quiz.question: In a free market economy, a key reason incomes are unequal is that:
options: wages are highest in the jobs most useful to society
owners of capital and land receive profit and rent
goods are rationed by price rather than by need
taxes are levied only on income from work
quiz.explanation: Income comes from owning assets as well as from work, and ownership is unequal, so owners of capital and land receive profit and rent that others do not. Pay follows the demand for and supply of each skill, not how useful a job is: care work is vital, but many people can do it. Rationing by price decides who gets goods once incomes differ; it does not make incomes differ. Market economies also tax profits, rent and property, not only wages.

practice.question: Define the term 'relative poverty'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two marks means two separate points. Say what the poor are compared with, and then how the benchmark is set — a definition that could equally describe absolute poverty earns only half.
Relative poverty is having an income so far below the typical income of one's own society that a person cannot share its normal way of life (1 mark). It is measured against a line set as a fraction of median income, commonly 50% or 60% (1 mark). "Being poorer than the rich" does not earn the second mark: the comparison is with the median, not the top.

practice.question: In a country, median income is $8.00 a day. The relative poverty line is set at 60% of median income. Calculate the relative poverty line. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Calculate asks for the working as well as the answer. Before any arithmetic, decide which figure the percentage is applied to, and give the answer in the units the question uses.
Relative poverty line = 60% × median = 0.6 × $8.00 (1 mark) = $4.80 a day (1 mark). Dividing the median by 0.6, or taking 40% of it, are the usual errors.

practice.question: Explain how an increase in welfare benefits paid to the poorest households could reduce relative poverty. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
An Explain wants linked stages. Start from what happens to the incomes of the poorest, then compare them with the benchmark that relative poverty is measured against, and ask whether that benchmark moves.
Knowledge: relative poverty is income below a line set at a fraction of median income (1 mark). Application: higher benefits raise the incomes of the poorest households directly (1 mark). Analysis: if the median is unchanged, because middle incomes do not receive the benefit, the relative line does not move (1 mark). Analysis: so some households rise above the line and the share in relative poverty falls (1 mark).

practice.question: Evaluate the view that economic growth is the most effective way to reduce absolute poverty in developing economies. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
An Evaluate wants chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and an informed judgement. Plan the strongest case for growth, then the alternatives the specification lists, and decide in advance what your judgement will turn on — the pattern of growth is the obvious place to start.
Level 1 describes growth or poverty with little explanation. Level 2 explains how growth raises jobs, wages and tax revenue so incomes cross the absolute line. Level 3 develops both sides with application: growth has been the main source of falling absolute poverty, but growth from capital-intensive sectors or concentrated in cities may bypass the poor, while benefits, aid, and education and training can reduce poverty more directly or more lastingly. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: growth is necessary for large, lasting falls in absolute poverty in most developing economies, but whether it is the most effective route depends on how labour-intensive it is and on whether the revenue it raises is spent on the poor.

practice.question: Analyse how structural changes in an economy may increase absolute poverty. (6 marks)
practice.guidance:
An Analyse wants depth: one route followed through several linked stages. Decide first what kind of structural change you will use, because the workers affected and the reason they cannot move depend on it.
Knowledge: structural change is a lasting shift in the industries an economy relies on (1 mark). Application: for example, cheaper imports close a country's textile mills (1 mark). Analysis, first stage: the mill workers lose their jobs, and their skills fit no growing industry nearby (1 mark). Analysis, second stage: they move into informal work or unemployment at much lower incomes (1 mark). Analysis, third stage: shops and suppliers in the mill towns lose customers, spreading the loss of income (1 mark). Analysis, final stage: more households fall below the fixed absolute poverty line (1 mark).

practice.question: On a Lorenz curve diagram for a country, the area below the Lorenz curve is 0.32. Ten years later it has fallen to 0.27. Calculate the Gini coefficient in each year and the change between them. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Calculate asks for workings. Write the formula for the Gini coefficient in words first, and note which area the question gives you: you need the other one before you can divide.
Area between the curve and the line of equality = 0.50 − 0.32 = 0.18 (1 mark). Gini = 0.18 ÷ 0.50 = 0.36 (1 mark). Ten years later the area is 0.50 − 0.27 = 0.23, so Gini = 0.23 ÷ 0.50 = 0.46 (1 mark). The Gini coefficient has risen by 0.10, so inequality has increased (1 mark).

practice.question: Examine two causes of inequality in income between countries. (8 marks)
practice.guidance:
An Examine wants chains of reasoning and a brief assessment, so save room for a judgement. Choose two causes that work through different channels, and for each follow it through to output per worker.
Level 1 names causes with little explanation. Level 2 explains one cause in a chain: for example, poorer countries have less capital and infrastructure per worker, so output and wages per worker are lower. Level 3 develops two causes with application — for example, capital and skills per worker, and dependence on volatile primary exports or weak institutions that deter investment. The brief assessment that lifts an answer to the top of the range weighs which cause matters more, and for which kind of economy: a commodity exporter with honest government faces a different binding constraint from a country held back by conflict or corruption.

practice.question: Discuss the likely impact of high income inequality on enterprise and savings in an economy. (14 marks)
practice.guidance:
A Discuss wants chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and a critical assessment. Treat enterprise and savings separately, give each a case for inequality and a case against, and decide what your judgement will depend on — the degree of inequality is the obvious place to start.
Level 1 describes inequality with little explanation. Level 2 explains one effect: the prospect of large profits rewards entrepreneurs for risk, or richer households save a larger share of income. Level 3 develops both impacts on both sides with application: inequality can reward enterprise and raise total saving, but extreme inequality leaves the poor unable to borrow to start firms, and savings by the rich may leave the country or buy existing assets rather than fund new investment, while the poor have no savings to fall back on. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: moderate inequality may strengthen incentives and saving, but beyond some point it wastes talent at the bottom, and the outcome depends on access to credit and on where the rich put their savings.

practice.question: Evaluate the view that a free market economy inevitably increases inequality. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
An Evaluate wants chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and an informed judgement. Decide first which features of a market economy create inequality, then what can offset them, so that the word "inevitably" is what your conclusion tests.
Level 1 describes capitalism or inequality with little explanation. Level 2 explains how private ownership and market-set pay lead to unequal incomes. Level 3 develops both sides with application: returns to capital, inheritance and rewards for scarce skills widen gaps, and technology and globalisation have added to them; against that, market-led growth has cut absolute poverty on a huge scale, competition erodes profits, rising demand for labour lifts wages, and market economies with strong taxes, benefits and public services have far lower inequality. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: a free market tends to create inequality, but how much remains is not inevitable — it depends on what the state does and on access to education.

practice.question: Evaluate the extent to which economic development reduces inequality within a country. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
An Evaluate wants chains of reasoning, different viewpoints and an informed judgement. Start from the Kuznets hypothesis, because the evaluation of this question is the evidence for and against it.
Level 1 describes development with little explanation. Level 2 explains the Kuznets hypothesis: inequality rises as workers move from farming to better-paid industry, then falls as most have moved and schooling spreads. Level 3 develops the evidence on both sides with application: some economies followed the curve, but several East Asian economies industrialised with stable inequality after land reform and mass schooling, and inequality has risen again in many high-income countries as technology and globalisation reward skills and capital. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement: development creates the means to reduce inequality — schooling, tax systems, better jobs — but whether it does depends on policy, not on the level of income alone.

flashcards.front: What is absolute poverty?
flashcards.back: An income too low to meet basic needs — food, safe water, shelter, clothing — measured against a fixed line.

flashcards.front: What is relative poverty?
flashcards.back: An income far below the typical income of one's own society, measured against a line set as a fraction (often 50% or 60%) of median income.

flashcards.front: What is the World Bank's international poverty line?
flashcards.back: $3.00 a day per person at 2021 purchasing power parity.

flashcards.front: What is the headcount ratio?
flashcards.back: The share of the population living below a poverty line.

flashcards.front: What does the poverty gap measure?
flashcards.back: The depth of poverty: how far below the poverty line the incomes of poor people fall.

flashcards.front: What does the Multidimensional Poverty Index count?
flashcards.back: Deprivations in health, schooling and living standards, such as clean water and electricity, rather than income.

flashcards.front: Why is relative poverty not the same as inequality?
flashcards.back: It compares the bottom with the median. If only the richest gain, inequality rises but the median and relative poverty do not change.

flashcards.front: What does evenly shared growth do to absolute and relative poverty?
flashcards.back: Absolute poverty falls as incomes cross the fixed line; relative poverty is unchanged because the median rises in step.

flashcards.front: Why do education and training reduce poverty slowly?
flashcards.back: Skills take years to build and raise income only when there are jobs that need them.

flashcards.front: How do welfare benefits change poverty?
flashcards.back: They raise the incomes of the poor directly, cutting poverty quickly if they reach the poor and are large enough.

flashcards.front: How can a change in tax structure raise poverty?
flashcards.back: Shifting tax onto spending on essentials takes a larger share of poor households' income, since they spend almost all of it.

flashcards.front: How can structural change increase poverty?
flashcards.back: A declining industry leaves workers whose skills and location fit no growing industry, so they fall into unemployment or informal work.

flashcards.front: Give the two routes by which aid can reduce poverty.
flashcards.back: Directly, through transfers and services for the poor; indirectly, through infrastructure that raises output and jobs.

flashcards.front: Name four channels through which conflict causes poverty.
flashcards.back: Lost incomes, destroyed assets, displacement of people, and collapsed public services.

flashcards.front: Distinguish income from wealth.
flashcards.back: Income is a flow received over time; wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time, net of debts.

flashcards.front: What does a Lorenz curve plot?
flashcards.back: The cumulative percentage of income against the cumulative percentage of the population, ranked from poorest.

flashcards.front: What is the line of equality?
flashcards.back: The diagonal on a Lorenz diagram, showing a distribution in which everyone has the same income.

flashcards.front: How is the Gini coefficient calculated?
flashcards.back: The area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve divided by the whole area under the line of equality.

flashcards.front: What do Gini coefficients of 0 and 1 mean?
flashcards.back: Zero: perfect equality. One: a single person receives all the income.

flashcards.front: Give two limitations of the Gini coefficient.
flashcards.back: Different distributions can share one value, so it hides where inequality lies; and survey data miss the very richest.

flashcards.front: Give three causes of income inequality within a country.
flashcards.back: Differences in skills and education, unemployment and informal work, and discrimination.

flashcards.front: Why does wealth concentrate over time?
flashcards.back: It is inherited, and returns on assets can grow faster than wages when reinvested.

flashcards.front: Give three causes of inequality between countries.
flashcards.back: Differences in capital and skills per worker, weak institutions, and dependence on primary exports.

flashcards.front: How can inequality strengthen incentives?
flashcards.back: The prospect of higher pay or profit rewards training, effort and risk-taking.

flashcards.front: How can extreme inequality weaken enterprise?
flashcards.back: The poor have no savings or collateral, so they cannot borrow to start firms, and their talent is wasted.

flashcards.front: How does inequality affect total saving?
flashcards.back: The rich save a larger share of income, so inequality can raise saving — though it may go abroad, and the poor are left with no buffer.

flashcards.front: How does inequality affect education?
flashcards.back: Poor families afford less and worse schooling, so inequality is handed on to the next generation.

flashcards.front: How does inequality drive migration?
flashcards.back: Income gaps pull people from poor regions to cities and from poor countries to rich ones.

flashcards.front: Why is life expectancy lower among the poor?
flashcards.back: Worse diets, housing, water and working conditions, and less access to health care.

flashcards.front: State the Kuznets hypothesis.
flashcards.back: As income per head rises, inequality first rises and then falls: an inverted U.

flashcards.front: Give one piece of evidence against the Kuznets hypothesis.
flashcards.back: Several East Asian economies industrialised fast without inequality rising sharply, after land reform and mass schooling.

flashcards.front: Why does a free market economy tend to create inequality?
flashcards.back: Incomes follow ownership of assets and the market value of skills, and returns on wealth accumulate.

mistakes.title: Confusing relative poverty with inequality
mistakes.looks_like: "The rich got richer, so relative poverty rose."
mistakes.why: Relative poverty compares the bottom with the median. A richer top raises inequality and leaves the median, the relative line and the number below it unchanged.
mistakes.instead: Say what happened to incomes at the bottom compared with the middle. Use the Gini coefficient for inequality and the relative headcount for relative poverty.

mistakes.title: Saying growth reduces "poverty" without saying which kind
mistakes.why: Evenly shared growth reduces absolute poverty and leaves relative poverty unchanged; growth that bypasses the poor reduces neither.
mistakes.instead: Name the measure — absolute or relative — and the pattern of growth that makes it fall.

mistakes.title: Swapping the axes of the Lorenz curve
mistakes.looks_like: Cumulative income along the bottom and population up the side.
mistakes.why: The Lorenz curve ranks people along the horizontal axis and shows the cumulative share of income they receive on the vertical axis.
mistakes.instead: Label the horizontal axis "cumulative % of population" and the vertical axis "cumulative % of income", then draw the diagonal as the line of equality.

mistakes.title: Drawing the Lorenz curve above the line of equality
mistakes.looks_like: A curve that bows up and to the left of the diagonal.
mistakes.why: The poorest x% of people can never receive more than x% of income, so the curve always lies on or below the diagonal.
mistakes.instead: Start at the origin, sag below the diagonal, and finish at the top right corner.

mistakes.title: Reading the Gini coefficient as a poverty rate
mistakes.looks_like: "A Gini of 0.4 means 40% of people are poor."
mistakes.why: The Gini coefficient is a ratio of two areas on the Lorenz diagram. It measures how unequally income is shared, not how many people are poor.
mistakes.instead: Say that a higher coefficient means a more unequal distribution, and use a headcount ratio for the number in poverty.

mistakes.title: Treating income and wealth as the same
mistakes.looks_like: "Wealth inequality is when some people earn more than others."
mistakes.why: Earnings are income, a flow. Wealth is the stock of assets owned. The two are linked but can differ sharply for the same household.
mistakes.instead: Define each by its flow or stock nature and give an example, then say which one a figure measures.

mistakes.title: Drawing the Kuznets curve against time, or as a U
mistakes.looks_like: A U-shaped curve with years along the horizontal axis.
mistakes.why: The hypothesis links inequality to the level of income per head, not to the passing of time, and it has inequality rising first and falling later: an inverted U.
mistakes.instead: Put income per head on the horizontal axis and inequality (for example the Gini coefficient) on the vertical, and draw a hump that rises and then falls.

diagrams.title: Development, Capitalism and Inequality
diagrams.description: IAL 4.3.4 · 2e and 2f: the Kuznets hypothesis that inequality rises and then falls as income per head grows, and how much of each group's income comes from owning assets in a market economy.
checklist: Early: most people farm on similar low incomes
Middle: some move to better-paid industry and the gap widens
Later: schooling spreads and the gap narrows
In a market economy, profit, rent and interest go mostly to those who own assets

chains.title: Why a richer top does not change relative poverty
steps: Marenda's median income is $6.00 a day, so the relative line is $3.60 and 30% of people are below it.
The richest two tenths gain: their incomes rise to $16.40 and $37.00.
The Gini coefficient rises from 0.39 to 0.49: inequality has increased.
The median is still $6.00, so the relative line has not moved.
The share below it is still 30%: relative poverty is unchanged.
chains.result: Relative poverty compares the bottom with the middle, and inequality measures the whole spread. They can move separately, which is why a question on one should never be answered with the other.

chains.title: Growth or benefits: which poverty falls?
steps: Today 20% of Marenda's people are below $3.00 and 30% below the relative line.
Growth of 25% for everyone: absolute poverty falls to 10%; relative stays 30%.
Instead, a $0.90 benefit to the poorest three tenths: absolute falls to 10%, relative to 20%.
The benefit costs $5.4 million a day, raised by a $2.70 tax on each of the richest tenth.
chains.result: Growth shared evenly moves the bottom up and the median up together. A targeted transfer moves only the bottom, so it can cut relative poverty as well — at a cost someone must pay.

chains.title: How a civil war deepens poverty
steps: Fighting closes markets and stops farming, so incomes collapse.
Homes, tools, livestock and roads are destroyed.
Families flee, losing their land and work.
Clinics and schools close as spending moves to the army.
In Marenda, a 30% fall in the poorer half's incomes takes absolute poverty from 20% to 40%.
chains.result: Conflict hits every channel of income at once, and its effects on schooling, assets and investment last long after the fighting ends.

chains.title: The Kuznets hypothesis, stage by stage
steps: Most people farm on similar low incomes: inequality is low.
Industry grows and pays more; some workers move to the towns.
The gap between modern and traditional sectors widens: inequality rises.
Most workers have moved, schooling spreads and pay at the bottom rises.
Tax and benefit systems develop: inequality falls.
chains.result: The curve is a hypothesis about development and inequality. Economies that combined industrialisation with land reform and mass schooling did not see the rise, and inequality has risen again in many rich countries.

evaluation.title: Is growth enough to end poverty?
evaluation.content: Growth has done more than anything else to reduce absolute poverty, but it does not reduce relative poverty unless the bottom gains faster than the middle. The pattern of growth matters more than its rate. Labour-intensive growth that raises wages at the bottom cuts poverty far more than growth from a mine or an oil field, and the tax revenue growth brings reduces poverty only if it is spent on the poor.

evaluation.title: How much inequality is too much?
evaluation.content: Some inequality rewards training, effort and enterprise. Beyond some point, it wastes talent and weakens the economy. Extreme inequality shuts the poor out of credit and schooling, shortens lives and drives out skilled workers. A strong evaluation asks how large the gap is, whether people can move up, and whether the rich earned their position by producing or by owning.

evaluation.title: Which measure answers the question?
evaluation.content: Absolute poverty, relative poverty, the poverty gap, wealth and the Gini coefficient measure different things, and data on one cannot answer a question about another. Name the measure before judging the trend. A country can cut absolute poverty while inequality rises, and a Gini coefficient for income says nothing about wealth.
